exam: A patient with diabetes presents with a painful, swollen foot ulcer and a WBC of 11 000 – what is your next step? — Assess for deep infection, obtain wound culture if possible, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Gram‑negatives and consider imaging.

You see a young adult with rapidly spreading erythema, severe pain, and crepitus on the thigh – which diagnosis is most likely and why? — Necrotizing fasciitis; pain out of proportion, gas on exam, systemic toxicity.
Why is amoxicillin‑clavulanate preferred for uncomplicated cellulitis in this setting? — Covers common streptococci and MSSA, also anaerobes common in tropical wounds.
A patient with a known MRSA colonisation develops an abscess – which oral regimen would you choose and why? — Clindamycin or TMP‑SMX; both active against MRSA and have good tissue penetration.
What are the key indications for surgical referral in SSTI? — Abscess requiring drainage, necrotizing fasciitis, gas in tissues, failure to improve after 24 h of antibiotics.
How does HIV infection alter your management of SSTI? — Higher risk of atypical organisms and poor healing; broaden coverage, monitor for opportunistic pathogens, ensure CD4 count assessment.
Explain why a normal CRP does not rule out necrotizing fasciitis. — Early disease may not yet trigger a systemic inflammatory response; clinical judgment supersedes labs.
What supportive measures are essential in a patient with severe cellulitis and sepsis? — IV fluids, analgesia, glucose control, oxygen if needed, and early broad‑spectrum antibiotics.
ai.title: Skin and Soft Tissue Infections
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Skin and soft tissue infections (SSTIs) range from mild cellulitis to life‑threatening necrotizing fasciitis. In low‑resource settings, common pathogens and limited diagnostics shape management.

sections.p: SSTIs are infections of the skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia or muscle. They are classified by depth (superficial vs deep) and severity (non‑purulent, purulent, necrotizing).

b: Rapid spread, pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity = severe/deep infection
Risk factors: diabetes, HIV, peripheral vascular disease, trauma, traditional herbal injections
sections.p: Diagnosis relies on history, exam and simple bedside tools; severity guides admission and surgical urgency.

b: Empiric therapy must cover both Gram‑positive and Gram‑negative organisms when resources allow
Early surgical drainage prevents progression to necrotizing disease
sections.p: In East African hospitals, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes dominate, but polymicrobial infections with Gram‑negative bacilli are common in diabetic foot and trauma.

t.b: Identifies organism type; guides antibiotic choice when culture unavailable
Confirms pathogen and resistance; not essential for uncomplicated cellulitis
Elevated WBC >12 000 suggests bacterial infection; neutrophilia supports bacterial cause
Detects gas in soft tissues → suggests necrotizing fasciitis or gas gangrene
Distinguishes abscess from cellulitis; guides drainage

b: First‑line oral for non‑purulent cellulitis: amoxicillin‑clavulanate (covers MSSA, streptococci, anaerobes)
If MRSA risk (prior infection, community prevalence): add clindamycin or TMP‑SMX
Purulent infections: incision & drainage plus same antibiotics
Necrotizing fasciitis: urgent broad‑spectrum IV (e.g., carbapenem + clindamycin) + surgical debridement
Supportive: analgesia, fluid resuscitation, glucose control in diabetics
sections.p: Treat the pathogen, control inflammation, and prevent complications. Surgical intervention is mandatory for abscesses and necrotizing disease.

b: DVT: unilateral leg swelling, positive Homan’s sign, Doppler needed
Gout: acute joint pain, tophi, uric acid elevation
Viral exanthem: diffuse rash, fever, no localized warmth
sections.p: Distinguish SSTIs from deep vein thrombosis, gouty arthritis, cellulitis‑like viral exanthems, and allergic cellulitis.

b: Pain out of proportion is more reliable than lab values for necrotizing disease
sections.p: Normal WBC does not exclude severe infection in immunocompromised patients; early necrotizing fasciitis may have modest labs.

b: Always assess pain severity, skin changes, and systemic signs first
State why you would choose or avoid a drug (e.g., clindamycin for toxin suppression)
sections.p: Examiners test your systematic approach, recognition of red flags, and rational antibiotic selection.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly expanding erythema, severe pain, fever >38.5 °C, hypotension, altered mental status, gas on X‑ray, or necrotic skin
